questions.question: What is mocking in unit testing and why do we need it?
questions.title: What is Mocking in Unit Testing | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: Mocking replaces a real dependency with a controlled fake that you configure to return specific values. It isolates the class under test from its dependencies—database, external APIs, file system—so you test only the unit's logic, not its dependencies.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that mocking is fundamentally about isolation and testing boundaries, not about making tests easier to pass.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking mocking is a shortcut to avoid writing real implementations, missing that it's about decoupling test scope from external systems.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain a concrete scenario where a failing database connection would break hundreds of unit tests if dependencies weren't mocked, showing you understand the practical need.

sections.title: Why Mocking Exists: Testing in Isolation
sections.content: **Mocking** is the practice of replacing real dependencies with fake objects you control during testing. Imagine testing a **UserService** that saves data to a database and sends an email. Without mocking, every test would need a live database and email server running—slow, brittle, and dependent on external infrastructure. Mocking lets you say "when the repository is called, return this user object" without touching a real database. **The core purpose is isolation**: you test whether UserService correctly calls its dependencies and handles their responses, not whether PostgreSQL works or SMTP delivers mail. Think of mocking like testing a light switch by replacing the bulb with a test harness that reports "I received power" instead of actually illuminating a room. You verify the switch's wiring logic, not the bulb's physics. **Isolation** means fast tests (milliseconds, not seconds), **deterministic** results (no flaky network timeouts), and **focused** failures (if UserService breaks, only its tests fail, not fifty integration tests).

sections.title: Mocking a Repository Dependency
Key Points
content: **Isolation**: mocking decouples the unit under test from external systems like databases, APIs, or file systems so tests run independently
**Speed**: mocked tests execute in milliseconds because no I/O operations occur; a full test suite with thousands of unit tests finishes in seconds
**Determinism**: real databases can be down or slow; mocked dependencies return exactly what you configure every time, eliminating flaky tests
**Focus**: when a test fails, you know the problem is in the class under test, not in a dependency twenty layers deep
**Control**: you can simulate error conditions (network timeout, null result, exception) that are hard to reproduce with real systems
**Mockito syntax**: when(mock.method()).thenReturn(value) configures behavior; verify(mock).method() asserts the method was called
**Not a replacement**: mocking doesn't eliminate the need for integration tests that verify real components work together end-to-end

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Mocking is when you replace a real dependency with a fake one that you control during testing. Let's say I'm testing an order service that calls a repository to fetch order data. Without mocking, I'd need a real database running for every test, which is slow and fragile. With mocking, I can say when the repository's findById method is called, just return this specific order object. That way I'm only testing whether my service correctly processes the order, not whether the database works. The whole point is isolation. If the service has a bug, only that test fails. If I used a real database and it went down, hundreds of unrelated tests would suddenly break. A common mistake freshers make is thinking mocking is just about making tests easier. It's really about separating concerns so each test has a single reason to fail. You'd mock external APIs, databases, email senders, anything with side effects. You wouldn't mock simple value objects or the class you're actually testing. That last point trips people up. If you mock the thing you're testing, you're not testing anything real anymore.

questions.question: What is Mockito and how do you add it to a Spring Boot project?
questions.title: Mockito Setup Spring Boot | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Mockito is the standard Java mocking library. In Spring Boot, spring-boot-starter-test includes Mockito automatically. Add at-ExtendsWith MockitoExtension.class to your test class to enable at-Mock and at-InjectMocks annotations.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical setup knowledge—can you use Mockito in a real Spring Boot project without fumbling with dependencies or configuration?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Manually adding Mockito as a separate Maven dependency when spring-boot-starter-test already includes it, creating version conflicts.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that spring-boot-starter-test uses test scope, so Mockito never pollutes production artifacts, and name the specific JUnit 5 extension class.

sections.title: Mockito: The Standard Java Mocking Framework
sections.content: **Mockito** is the de facto mocking library in the Java ecosystem, used by millions of projects. It provides a clean API for creating mock objects, stubbing method behavior, and verifying interactions. In **Spring Boot**, you don't need to add Mockito manually—**spring-boot-starter-test** bundles it along with JUnit 5, AssertJ, and other testing utilities. When you declare spring-boot-starter-test in your pom.xml or build.gradle with **test scope**, Mockito comes along automatically. The key integration point is the **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** annotation from JUnit 5. This extension activates Mockito's annotation processing, allowing you to use **@Mock** to create mock objects and **@InjectMocks** to inject those mocks into the class under test. Before JUnit 5, you'd use **@RunWith(MockitoJUnitRunner.class)** with JUnit 4, but the modern approach uses the extension model. The beauty of this setup is zero configuration: add the starter, annotate your test class, and Mockito is ready.

sections.title: Adding Mockito to a Spring Boot Test
Key Points
content: **spring-boot-starter-test**: this single dependency includes Mockito, JUnit 5, AssertJ, Hamcrest, and Spring test utilities; no need to add Mockito separately
**test scope**: spring-boot-starter-test is declared with scope test in Maven or testImplementation in Gradle, ensuring Mockito stays out of production builds
**@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)**: JUnit 5 extension that initializes Mockito before each test method runs; replaces the older at-RunWith for JUnit 4
**@Mock annotation**: tells Mockito to create a mock instance of the annotated field; the mock starts with no behavior configured
**@InjectMocks annotation**: tells Mockito to create a real instance of the class and inject all at-Mock fields into it via constructor or setters
**Manual initialization**: if you don't use the extension, call MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this) in a setup method, though the extension approach is cleaner
**Version compatibility**: Spring Boot 3.x uses Mockito 5.x; Spring Boot 2.x uses Mockito 4.x; the API is mostly backward-compatible

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Mockito is the most widely used mocking framework in Java. It's kind of the industry standard. In a Spring Boot project, you don't need to add Mockito as a separate dependency because it's already included in spring-boot-starter-test. That's the starter you add for all your testing libraries. It bundles Mockito, JUnit 5, AssertJ, and a few others. To use Mockito in a test class, you annotate the class with at-ExtendsWith MockitoExtension.class. That's a JUnit 5 extension that activates Mockito's annotation processing. Then you can use at-Mock to create mock objects and at-InjectMocks to inject those mocks into the class you're testing. A common mistake is adding Mockito manually in your POM file when it's already there. That can cause version conflicts because Spring Boot manages the version for you. One thing that's worth mentioning is that spring-boot-starter-test uses test scope, so Mockito is only available during testing. It won't end up in your production JAR. That's important because mocking libraries have no place in production code.

questions.question: When should you NOT mock a dependency?
questions.title: When Not to Mock | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Don't mock value objects, simple utilities, or classes you own that have no side effects. Don't mock the class under test itself. Don't mock thin wrappers that are trivially tested with real implementation. Over-mocking produces tests that test the test setup, not the code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Testing judgment—knowing the limits of mocking is as important as knowing how to use it; good engineers know when NOT to apply a tool.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mocking everything including simple value classes, DTOs, and pure functions, which wastes setup time and tests nothing real.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the 'mock only what you don't own' guideline from Growing Object-Oriented Software and explain when integration tests are better than heavily mocked unit tests.

sections.title: The Limits of Mocking: When Real is Better
sections.content: **Not every dependency should be mocked.** The guideline from *Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests* is **only mock types you don't own**—external APIs, databases, messaging systems. Value objects like **LocalDate**, **BigDecimal**, or your own **Money** record are cheap to construct and have no side effects; mocking them adds complexity with zero benefit. **Don't mock the class under test itself**—if you mock UserService while testing UserService, you're not testing anything. Don't mock **simple utilities** like StringUtils or MathHelper that have deterministic logic and no I/O. Don't mock **DTOs** or **domain entities** that are just data containers. Over-mocking creates tests that verify mock setup rather than real behavior. If 80% of your test is configuring mocks and 20% is actual assertions, you've crossed into **testing the test**. Integration tests with real dependencies (even in-memory databases like H2) are often faster to write and more valuable than heavily mocked unit tests.

sections.title: Step 1: Does It Have Side Effects?
sections.content: Ask whether the dependency interacts with external systems or mutable shared state. **Mock**: a repository that writes to PostgreSQL, a REST client calling an external API, a message publisher sending to Kafka, a file writer touching the filesystem. These have **side effects** you can't control in a unit test. **Don't mock**: a calculator class that adds numbers, a formatter that converts dates to strings, a record with getters, an immutable list. These are **pure functions** or **value objects** with no side effects. Testing them with real instances is trivial and proves the integration works. A rough heuristic: if constructing the real object requires **new** and zero arguments or simple parameters, don't mock it.

sections.title: Step 2: Do You Own the Code?
sections.content: If you control the source code of a class and it's part of your domain logic, **prefer real instances in tests**. Mocking your own domain classes couples tests to implementation details. If you refactor the class, mocked tests break even though behavior didn't change. **Don't mock**: your own domain entities like Order or Customer, your own value objects like Address or EmailAddress, your own service classes when testing a higher-level orchestrator (consider integration tests instead). **Mock**: third-party libraries you don't control like Spring's RestTemplate, AWS SDK clients, Apache HttpClient, or javax.mail.Transport. The rationale: you can't change external code if it's wrong, so mocking is your only option. Your own code should be testable with real objects if designed well.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Value objects**: classes like LocalDate, BigDecimal, records, or immutable DTOs are cheap to construct and have no side effects; always use real instances
**The class under test**: never mock the object you're testing; you'd be verifying mock behavior instead of real logic
**Pure functions**: utility methods that transform data without I/O or state changes don't need mocking; they're deterministic and fast
**Domain entities**: your own Order, Customer, Product classes should generally be real in tests; mocking them couples tests to internal structure
**Over-mocking smell**: if test setup is longer than the test body and full of when/thenReturn chains, you've probably mocked too much
**Integration test threshold**: when you're mocking five or more dependencies, consider writing an integration test with real components instead
**Only mock types you don't own**: guideline from GOOS; mock external APIs and infrastructure, not your own domain logic

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: You shouldn't mock everything. There's a guideline from the book Growing Object-Oriented Software that says only mock types you don't own. That means mock external systems like databases or REST APIs, but don't mock your own domain classes. If you're testing an order service and you mock the Order object itself, you're not really testing anything. The order is just data. Use a real instance. Same with value objects. Don't mock LocalDate or BigDecimal or a simple record. They're trivial to construct and have no side effects. Another case is pure functions. If you have a utility that formats strings or calculates totals, don't mock it. Just call it. The test will be simpler and you'll actually verify the integration works. A big red flag is when your test setup is twenty lines of when-thenReturn calls and the actual test is three lines. That's over-mocking. You're testing the mock configuration, not the code. Sometimes it means you need an integration test instead. Use an in-memory database or a real Spring context. It's slower but way more valuable. The rule of thumb is mock things you can't control—external APIs, databases, message queues—and use real objects for everything you own.

questions.question: What is the difference between mocking and stubbing?
questions.title: Mocking vs Stubbing Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Stubbing configures a fake to return a specific value using when-thenReturn. Mocking in the verification sense asserts that a method was called using verify. Mockito objects are both—they can stub return values AND verify interactions. The terms are often used interchangeably in casual speech.

interviewer_intent.testing: Precise vocabulary around test doubles and whether you know the technical distinction even though Mockito blurs the line.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using mock and stub interchangeably without knowing that stub is about return values and mock is about call verification.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Reference Gerard Meszaros's test double taxonomy and explain that Mockito's unified approach is pragmatic but technically a mock is a stub with verification.

sections.title: Stubbing vs Mocking: Two Sides of a Fake Object
sections.content: In testing theory, **stubbing** and **mocking** are distinct operations, though Mockito combines them. **Stubbing** means configuring a fake object to return a specific value when a method is called—**when(repo.findById(1L)).thenReturn(order)**. You're defining the fake's behavior so the test can proceed. **Mocking** in the strict sense means asserting that a method was called with specific arguments—**verify(repo).save(order)**. You're checking that the code under test interacted with the dependency correctly. **Gerard Meszaros** in *xUnit Test Patterns* classifies test doubles into five types: **dummy** (passed but never used), **stub** (returns canned answers), **fake** (working implementation but unsuitable for production), **spy** (records calls), and **mock** (verifies interactions). Mockito objects are technically **spies**—they can stub AND verify. The library's name "Mockito" reflects common usage where "mock" means any test double, even though purists distinguish them.

sections.title: When to Use Each Approach
sections.content: **Use stubbing** when the code under test calls a dependency and uses the returned value to make a decision. Example: an order service calls a repository to fetch an order, then calculates a discount based on order total. Stub the repository to return a known order, then assert the discount is correct. **Use mocking (verify)** when the code under test calls a dependency purely for side effects and doesn't use the return value. Example: an event publisher sends a notification after an order is placed. You stub the publisher to avoid real message sending, but you **verify** it was called with the correct event payload. Over-verification is a common mistake: verifying every getter call creates brittle tests. Only verify calls that represent **observable behavior changes**—writes, sends, deletes—not reads or queries.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Stubbing**: configuring return values with when-thenReturn so the test can proceed with controlled data; focuses on providing inputs
**Mocking (verification)**: asserting a method was called with verify; focuses on confirming side effects or interactions happened
**Mockito unifies both**: a single mock object can be stubbed for return values and verified for calls; no separate stub vs mock classes
**Test double taxonomy**: Gerard Meszaros defines five types—dummy, stub, fake, spy, mock—with distinct purposes; Mockito is technically a spy library
**State-based vs interaction-based**: stubbing supports state-based testing (assert final result); mocking supports interaction-based testing (assert calls made)
**Over-verification trap**: verifying every method call couples tests to implementation; only verify calls that represent observable behavior changes
**Common usage**: in everyday speech, developers say mock when they mean any test double; technically stub and mock are different but Mockito blurs the line

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Stubbing and mocking are two different things, though Mockito lets you do both with the same object. Stubbing is when you configure a fake dependency to return a specific value. Like when you say when the repository's findById method is called, return this order. You're setting up the behavior so your test can run. Mocking in the strict sense is when you verify that a method was actually called. You use verify to assert the code under test interacted with the dependency. So if you're testing a service that's supposed to save an order, you'd verify the repository's save method was called. Now here's the thing. Mockito's objects can do both. You can stub return values and verify calls on the same mock. That's super convenient. Technically, in the testing literature like Gerard Meszaros's book, these are different types of test doubles. A stub just provides answers. A mock verifies behavior. But in real projects, people use the word mock for everything. One thing to watch out for is over-verification. Don't verify every single method call. Only verify the side effects that matter, like saving to a database or sending a message. If you verify every getter, your tests become brittle and break whenever you refactor.

questions.question: What is the difference between a test double and a mock?
questions.title: Test Double vs Mock
questions.direct_answer: Test double is the umbrella term for any fake object used in testing; a mock is a specific type of test double that also verifies interactions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand testing vocabulary precisely and know that Mockito blurs some of these boundaries for pragmatic reasons.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using mock and test double interchangeably when they have distinct meanings in Martin Fowler's and Gerard Meszaros's taxonomies.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name all five categories of test doubles—dummy, stub, fake, spy, mock—and explain where Mockito fits (spy with mock-like verification).

sections.title: Test Doubles: The Full Taxonomy
sections.content: **Test double** is the umbrella term for any object that stands in for a real dependency during testing—coined by analogy to "stunt double" in movies. **Gerard Meszaros** and **Martin Fowler** classify test doubles into five types, each with a distinct purpose. A **dummy** is passed to satisfy method signatures but never used (like null or an empty object). A **stub** returns canned answers to calls during the test. A **fake** is a working implementation that takes shortcuts unsuitable for production (like an in-memory database). A **spy** records information about how it was called so you can assert on it later. A **mock** is pre-programmed with expectations about calls and fails the test if expectations aren't met. **Mockito** doesn't follow this taxonomy strictly. Mockito's objects are technically **spies** that can also verify like mocks. When you create a Mockito mock, it starts as a dumb stub (returns null by default), you stub methods to define behavior (making it stub-like), and you verify calls (making it mock-like). So Mockito is a pragmatic hybrid that calls everything a "mock" even though it's more accurately a spy.

rows: When you call verify on it

sections.title: When to Use Each Type of Test Double
sections.content: **Use a dummy** when a method signature requires an argument but your test doesn't care about it—pass null or an empty object. **Use a stub** when the code under test queries a dependency for data and you want to control the response—stub a repository to return a specific user. **Use a fake** when you need a lightweight working implementation for testing—use H2 in-memory database instead of PostgreSQL, or a fake email sender that logs messages to a list. **Use a spy** when you want to use the real object but also record how it was called—Mockito's spy wraps a real instance. **Use a mock** when the interaction itself is the behavior you're testing—verify that a notification was sent, an audit log was written, or a cache was invalidated. In Mockito, you use spy for real objects with verification and mock for fully fake objects.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Test double**: umbrella term from Gerard Meszaros covering any fake object used in testing; like stunt double in film
**Five types**: dummy (never used), stub (returns answers), fake (working but simplified), spy (records calls), mock (verifies expectations)
**Mock is specific**: a test double that asserts interactions happened; fails the test if expected calls don't occur
**Mockito's approach**: technically creates spies that can stub and verify; calls them mocks for simplicity and common usage
**Stub vs mock distinction**: stub provides data for state-based testing; mock verifies interactions for interaction-based testing
**Real-world usage**: developers often say mock when they mean any test double; precise terminology matters in interviews or design discussions
**Martin Fowler's article**: Mocks Aren't Stubs is the classic reference explaining the difference and when each style of testing is appropriate

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Test double is the general term for any kind of fake object you use in a test. It's like saying vehicle when you could mean car, truck, or motorcycle. A mock is one specific type of test double. The distinction comes from Gerard Meszaros's book on testing patterns. He defines five categories. A dummy is just passed around but never used. A stub returns hardcoded values. A fake is a real implementation that's simplified, like an in-memory database. A spy records how it was called so you can check later. And a mock is pre-programmed with expectations and fails the test if those expectations aren't met. Now here's where it gets practical. Mockito technically creates spies, not mocks, because you configure behavior after creation and optionally verify calls. But everyone calls them mocks anyway because that's the common usage. When you call Mockito.mock, you get an object that can act like a stub when you use when-thenReturn, and it acts like a mock when you use verify. The key thing for an interview is to know that test double is the umbrella term and mock is specific to verification. If someone asks about the difference, mention the five types and that Mockito blurs the lines for pragmatic reasons. That shows you know the theory and the practice.

questions.title: When Not to Use Mocking
questions.direct_answer: Avoid mocking value objects, the class under test itself, or any dependency so heavily that the test only exercises mock behavior rather than real logic.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the limits and pitfalls of over-mocking, not just how to create mocks; good judgment separates junior from mid-level engineers.

sections.title: When Mocking Becomes Counterproductive
sections.content: **Over-mocking** is when tests are so full of mock configuration that they verify the mocks, not the code. The clearest anti-pattern is **mocking the class under test**—if you're testing OrderService and you mock OrderService, you're not testing anything. Another mistake is **mocking value objects** like LocalDate, BigDecimal, or your own immutable DTOs. These have no side effects and cost nothing to instantiate. Mocking them adds lines of when-thenReturn for zero benefit. **Don't mock simple utilities** like StringUtils or Math.max. They're pure functions—deterministic, fast, no I/O. Use the real thing. **Don't mock your own domain entities** unless they're genuinely expensive to construct (rare). If you mock Customer, Order, Product in every test, you're coupling tests to internal structure. A refactor breaks all tests even though behavior didn't change. The guideline from *Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests*: **only mock types you don't own**. Mock external APIs, databases, message brokers. Use real objects for your own domain logic.

sections.title: Trade-offs of Mocking vs Real Objects
sections.content: **Pros of mocking**: isolation (no external dependencies), speed (no I/O), control (simulate errors easily), determinism (no flaky network calls). **Cons of mocking**: brittle tests (coupled to implementation details), false confidence (mocks return what you configure, not what production does), setup complexity (when-thenReturn chains longer than test body), missed integration bugs (real database constraints or API quirks aren't tested). **Pros of real objects**: tests prove actual integration works, simpler test code (no mock setup), refactoring-safe (tests break only if behavior changes), closer to production behavior. **Cons of real objects**: slower (real I/O takes milliseconds to seconds), less isolation (a database issue fails many tests), harder to test edge cases (can't easily simulate network timeout with real HttpClient). **The balance**: mock at architectural boundaries (database, external APIs), use real objects within your domain logic. If you find yourself mocking five collaborators for one test, consider an integration test with a real Spring context and in-memory database instead.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Never mock the class under test**: if you mock OrderService while testing OrderService, you're testing nothing; the mock returns what you told it to
**Don't mock value objects**: LocalDate, BigDecimal, immutable DTOs, records—these are trivial to construct and have no side effects
**Don't mock pure functions**: utility classes that transform data without I/O or shared state don't need mocking; use the real implementation
**Don't mock your own domain**: mocking Customer or Order entities couples tests to internal structure and breaks on refactoring
**Only mock types you don't own**: guideline from GOOS; mock external systems (database, API clients, message queues), not your own domain logic
**Integration test threshold**: if mocking more than 3-4 dependencies, consider writing an integration test with real components instead
**False confidence**: heavily mocked tests can pass even when production is broken because mocks behave exactly as configured, not as reality does

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: You should avoid mocking when the dependency is simple enough to use for real or when you're mocking so much that the test doesn't reflect reality anymore. The most obvious mistake is mocking the class you're actually testing. If you mock OrderService in a test for OrderService, you're not testing anything. The mock just returns what you told it to. Another case is value objects. Don't mock LocalDate or BigDecimal or a simple record. They're cheap to create and they don't have side effects. Just use the real thing. Same with pure utility functions. If you're testing a service that calls a string formatter, don't mock the formatter. It's deterministic and fast. You also shouldn't mock your own domain classes like Customer or Product unless they're genuinely expensive to construct, which is rare. If you mock them everywhere, your tests break whenever you refactor, even if behavior didn't change. There's a guideline from the book Growing Object-Oriented Software: only mock types you don't own. That means mock external APIs, databases, message systems. Use real objects for your own code. The big risk of over-mocking is false confidence. Your tests pass because the mocks behave exactly as you configured them, not because your code actually works in production. If you're spending more time setting up mocks than writing assertions, that's a smell. Consider an integration test instead.

questions.question: What is the difference between state-based testing and interaction-based testing, and where does mocking fit?
questions.title: State vs Interaction Testing
questions.direct_answer: State-based testing asserts on the final state of an object; interaction-based testing, where mocking lives, asserts that the right collaborators were called in the right way.

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of understanding of why mocking exists as a concept and when it's the appropriate testing strategy versus state verification.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating every test as interaction-based and over-verifying internal calls, making tests brittle and coupled to implementation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that interaction tests are fragile and should be reserved for side-effect boundaries like external APIs or messaging, not internal logic.

sections.title: Two Testing Philosophies: State vs Interaction
sections.content: **State-based testing** asserts on the final state of the object under test or its returned values—call a method, check the result or the object's fields. Example: call orderService.calculateTotal() and assert the returned value is 100.0. You're verifying **what** the code produces. **Interaction-based testing** asserts on how the object under test interacted with its collaborators—which methods were called, with what arguments, in what order. Example: call orderService.placeOrder() and verify that repository.save() was called once with the correct order. You're verifying **how** the code behaves. **Mocking lives in interaction-based testing** because mocks are designed to record and verify calls. The distinction originates from **Martin Fowler's** article *Mocks Aren't Stubs*. State-based tests are **classical TDD**—you test behavior through observable outputs. Interaction-based tests are **mockist TDD**—you test behavior through verified interactions. Both are valid, but over-reliance on interaction testing makes tests brittle: any implementation refactor breaks tests even if the final result is correct.

sections.title: When to Choose Each Approach
sections.content: **Use state-based testing** when the code under test produces a clear output or changes observable state. Examples: a calculator returns a sum, a validator returns true/false, a mapper transforms one object to another. The test calls the method and asserts on the result. This style is **refactoring-friendly**: you can change internal logic without breaking tests as long as the final output is correct. **Use interaction-based testing** when the code's purpose is to coordinate side effects with no meaningful return value. Examples: a controller receives a request and calls a service to persist data, an event handler publishes a message to Kafka, a scheduler triggers a batch job. The side effect IS the behavior, so you verify the interaction happened. **Prefer state-based by default**; reserve interaction testing for boundaries where side effects are the observable behavior. Over-verification of internal calls creates brittle tests.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **State-based testing**: asserts on final state or return values; verifies what the code produces; uses assertEquals, assertTrue on results
**Interaction-based testing**: asserts on calls to collaborators; verifies how the code behaves; uses verify in Mockito to check method calls
**Mocking's home**: interaction-based testing is where mocks shine because mocks record calls and verify expectations
**Classical vs mockist TDD**: Martin Fowler's terms; classical tests prefer state assertions and real objects; mockist tests prefer mocks and interaction verification
**Brittleness trade-off**: interaction tests break when you refactor implementation even if behavior is unchanged; state tests survive refactoring
**Side-effect boundaries**: interaction testing is appropriate for external APIs, databases, message queues where the call itself is the observable behavior
**Default to state-based**: verify outputs and final state by default; use interaction testing only when side effects are the primary behavior being tested

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: State-based testing is when you assert on the final result or the state of an object after you call a method. Like you call a calculator's add method and check that the result is ten. You're verifying what the code produces. Interaction-based testing is when you assert that the code called specific methods on its dependencies. You call a service's placeOrder method and verify that the repository's save method was called. You're verifying how the code behaves. Mocking fits into interaction-based testing because that's what mocks are designed for. You create a mock, configure it with when-thenReturn, and then verify it was called correctly. The distinction comes from Martin Fowler. He talks about classical versus mockist TDD. Classical prefers state assertions and real objects. Mockist prefers mocks and interaction verification. Both are valid but there's a trade-off. Interaction tests are brittle. If you refactor the internal implementation, the test breaks even though the final behavior is the same. State-based tests are more resilient to refactoring. They only care about the output. The rule of thumb is default to state-based testing. Use interaction testing at boundaries where side effects are the main behavior. Like verifying a message was published or a database write happened. Don't verify every internal method call. That couples your tests to implementation details and makes refactoring painful.

questions.question: How does over-mocking harm a test suite, and how do you recognise it?
questions.title: Over-Mocking Pitfalls
questions.direct_answer: Over-mocking means mocking classes you own and control, making tests pass even when real integration would fail, and tightly coupling tests to implementation details.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of the limits and risks of mocking; distinguishing engineers who understand when a tool is harmful from those who apply it everywhere.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mocking value objects, DTOs, or simple domain classes that have no side effects, resulting in tests that exercise mock configuration rather than code.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the 'only mock types you don't own' heuristic from Growing Object-Oriented Software and describe a concrete sign: test setup longer than test body.

sections.title: The Cost of Over-Mocking: False Confidence
sections.content: **Over-mocking** is when a test suite is so full of mocks that tests pass even when the real system is broken. The hallmark: test setup is longer than the test body, with chains of when-thenReturn configuring mock behavior that may not reflect production. **Example**: mocking a ProductRepository to return a product, mocking a PriceCalculator to return a price, mocking a DiscountService to return a discount, then asserting the final total. This test verifies mock orchestration, not real business logic. If ProductRepository's query is wrong in production, the test still passes. **Symptoms of over-mocking**: (1) mocking value objects like LocalDate or BigDecimal, (2) mocking the class under test itself, (3) mocking classes you own and control (domain entities, DTOs), (4) test suites with more verify statements than assertions, (5) tests that break on every refactor even when behavior is unchanged. **Steve Freeman and Nat Pryce** in *Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests* advocate: **only mock types you don't own**—external APIs, databases, message queues. Your own domain logic should be testable with real objects.

sections.title: Signs You've Crossed the Line into Over-Mocking
sections.content: **Sign 1: Test setup longer than test body**—if fifteen lines configure mocks and three lines make assertions, you're testing the test. **Sign 2: Mocking value objects**—when(clock.now()).thenReturn(fixedDate) is sensible; when(bigDecimal.add(any())).thenReturn(mockResult) is absurd. **Sign 3: Mocking your own domain classes**—mocking Customer, Order, Product means tests couple to internal structure. A field rename breaks fifty tests. **Sign 4: No integration tests**—unit tests with mocks verify interactions; integration tests verify components work together. If you have only mocked unit tests, you haven't proven the system functions. **Sign 5: Tests pass but production fails**—the ultimate symptom. Mocks return exactly what you configure, not what production does. If your stub returns a valid user but the real database query has a typo, tests pass and production breaks. **The fix**: use real objects for domain logic, reserve mocks for architectural boundaries, and supplement heavily mocked unit tests with integration tests that use real Spring contexts and in-memory databases.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Over-mocking definition**: mocking so many dependencies that tests verify mock behavior instead of real code; setup dwarfs assertions
**False confidence**: tests pass because mocks return configured values, not because production code is correct; integration bugs slip through
**Coupling to implementation**: mocking internal collaborators means tests break on refactoring even when behavior is unchanged
**Value object mistake**: mocking LocalDate, BigDecimal, immutable DTOs, or records is a red flag; these are cheap to construct
**Domain class mistake**: mocking your own Order, Customer, Product classes tightly couples tests to internal structure
**Only mock types you don't own**: GOOS heuristic; mock external systems (databases, APIs), use real objects for domain logic
**Recognition heuristic**: if test setup exceeds 10 lines or you have more when-thenReturn calls than assertions, consider an integration test

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Over-mocking is when you mock so many things that the test doesn't reflect reality anymore. You end up testing the mock configuration instead of the actual code. One clear sign is when your test setup is twenty lines of when-thenReturn calls and the actual test is three lines. That's a red flag. Another sign is mocking value objects or simple data classes. If you're mocking BigDecimal or LocalDate or a record, you've gone too far. These are trivial to construct and have no side effects. A big mistake freshers make is mocking their own domain classes. If you mock Order or Customer in every test, you're coupling tests to internal structure. Any refactor breaks all the tests even though the behavior didn't change. The harm is false confidence. Your tests pass because the mocks behave exactly as you configured them, not because the code actually works. If the real repository has a bug in its SQL query, your test won't catch it because you stubbed the repository to return a valid result. There's a guideline from the book Growing Object-Oriented Software: only mock types you don't own. That means mock external APIs, databases, message queues. Use real objects for your own domain logic. If you find yourself mocking five or more dependencies for one test, that's a sign you should write an integration test instead. Use a real Spring context with an in-memory database. It's slower but way more valuable.
